assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Speed
items.clue: How fast an object is moving, whatever its direction.

items.label: Distance
items.clue: How far an object moves along the path it actually travels.

questions.stem: A student walks 30 m due east along a corridor and then walks 30 m back to the point where she started. What are the distance she has travelled and her displacement?

options.text: Distance 60 m; displacement zero, as she ends where she began
Distance 60 m; displacement 60 m, as both measure her walk
Distance 60 m; displacement 30 m, the furthest point reached
Distance 30 m; displacement 30 m west, using the return leg

questions.explanation: Distance is measured along the whole path walked, 30 m + 30 m = 60 m. The straight line from start point to finish point has no length, so the displacement is zero.

questions.stem: Why is the speed of a car driven across a busy town rarely constant?

options.text: Cars are built to hold a single steady speed once moving
The driver keeps changing speed at junctions and bends
Speed can only change when the direction changes too
A speedometer shows the average speed of the trip

questions.explanation: The speed of a moving object is rarely constant: when people walk, run or travel in a car their speed is constantly changing.

questions.stem: A walker sets off from a car park, goes 3.0 km due east and then 4.0 km due north. Which of these correctly expresses her displacement from the car park?

options.text: 7.0 km, on a heading 37 degrees east of north
5.0 km, in a direction 37 degrees east of north
5.0 km, and no direction needs to be stated
1.0 km, due north of the car park she left

questions.explanation: The two legs are at right angles, so the magnitude is the square root of (3.0^2 + 4.0^2) = 5.0 km, and a displacement must also carry the direction of that straight line.

questions.stem: Which list gives factors that affect the speed at which a person can walk, run or cycle?

options.text: Fitness alone, as everybody else walks at 1.5 m/s
Terrain and distance only, as age has no effect on it
Age, fitness, terrain and the distance travelled
Only terrain, since a person's speed is fixed

questions.explanation: The specification lists age, terrain, fitness and distance travelled among the many factors affecting the speed at which a person can walk, run or cycle.

questions.stem: Which pair contains only scalar quantities?

options.text: Speed and velocity, as both describe how fast it goes
Distance and displacement, as both are lengths in metres
Distance and speed, as neither has a direction
Displacement and velocity, both having a size

questions.explanation: Distance is how far an object moves and speed is how fast it moves; neither involves direction, so both are scalars.

questions.stem: Which is the best estimate of the typical speed of a person walking?

options.text: 6.0 m/s, close to 22 km/h
15 m/s, or roughly 54 km/h
0.15 m/s, or about 0.5 km/h
1.5 m/s, or about 5 km/h

questions.explanation: The specification gives walking as about 1.5 m/s, which is roughly 5 km/h - a familiar walking pace.

questions.stem: Which quantity is only fully described when a direction is given as well as a number and a unit?

options.text: Distance, measured along the path
The time taken, measured in seconds
Speed, measured in metres per second
Displacement, a vector quantity

questions.explanation: Displacement is a vector: it is the straight-line distance from start to finish together with the direction of that line, so both parts must be stated.

questions.stem: A student is asked to use typical values for the speeds of a runner and a cyclist. Which pair should she use?

options.text: Running about 3 m/s and cycling about 6 m/s
Running about 6 m/s, cycling about 3 m/s
Running near 3 m/s, cycling near 3 m/s
Running 1.5 m/s, cycling about 6 m/s

questions.explanation: The specification gives running as about 3 m/s and cycling as about 6 m/s, roughly double the running value.

questions.stem: Which is the most sensible typical speed to quote for a car travelling along a motorway?

options.text: About 300 m/s, which is close to the speed of sound
About 30 m/s, which is roughly 70 miles per hour
About 10 m/s, a little faster than a cyclist
About 3 m/s, about a person's running pace

questions.explanation: A motorway speed of about 30 m/s is close to 70 mph and is the usual typical value quoted for a car.

questions.stem: Which statement about the speed of sound in air is correct?

options.text: It is fixed at 300 000 000 m/s in every case
It is always exactly 330 m/s, whatever the air
It varies, but a typical value is 330 m/s
It varies, but a typical value is 33 m/s

questions.explanation: The specification gives a typical value of 330 m/s and notes that the speed of sound, like the speed of the wind, varies.

questions.stem: A student sees a flash of lightning and hears the thunder 6.0 s later. Taking the speed of sound in air as 330 m/s, how far away was the lightning?
questions.explanation: Using distance travelled = speed × time, s = v t = 330 m/s × 6.0 s = 1980 m.

questions.stem: A train travels at a constant speed of 45 m/s. How long does it take to travel 9.0 km?
questions.explanation: Rearranging s = v t gives t = s / v. Converting 9.0 km to 9000 m, t = 9000 / 45 = 200 s.
